While you do get a number of commercial pilots from the military, a more common path is private pilot -> commercial pilot, multi-engine (roughly $15k - $20k depending on how you do it). You'll need to aquire an instrument rating and turbine rating along the way... more $$.  

You also need to accumulate about 1500 hours in the cockpit; a common solution for this is to become a CFI (certified flight instructor) and let students try to kill you for a few years. As an alternative, you could find a job mapping stuff like pipelines, be a co-pilot for a small freight operation, small aircraft charter tours, etc. You'd make anywhere from $20k to $45k doing this stuff. I knew a guy who went into crop dusting; he lilked it so much that he never did anything else. (Some people take out a big loan and do ab initio training directly into regionals.)  

Whichever way you go, you'd typically move into the right seat of a regional airline ($50k, if you're lucky), then left seat, then, after earning an ATP (airline transport pilot) license, some more training and seniority, you'd perform the same right-to-left evolution in bigger equipment. Then, when you're in your 40's, hopefully move into bigger jets / international long-haul for one of the big carriers.  

If you've made it this far and into the left seat of a big jet, you can finally start making some money- your union contract guarantees so many flight hours (I've heard of 800-1100) per year at > $160 / hour. By the time you make it here, however, you're an old guy.
